Tokugawa Yoshinobu
德川 慶喜 | image = 1867 Osaka Yoshinobu Tokugawa.jpg | caption = Tokugawa in 1867 | succession = Member of the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}} | reign-type = Tenure | reign = 1902–1910 | birth_date = {{birth date|1837|10|28}} | birth_place = {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}, Tokugawa Shogunate | death_date = {{death date and age|1913|11|22|1837|10|28}} | death_place = [[:en:Bunkyō, Tokyo|Bunkyō, Tokyo]], Empire Of Japan | burial_place = {{ill|Yanaka Cemetery|en|Yanaka Cemetery|WD=Q864387|lt=Yanaka Cemetery|1=Yanaka Cemetery}} | spouse = {{ill|Ichijo Mikako|jp|一条美賀子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichijo Mikako|qq=}} | house = [[Tokugawa clan]] | father = [[Tokugawa Nariaki]] | mother = {{ill|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|en|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|WD=Q8944971|lt=Arisugawa Yoshiko|1=Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)}} | signature = Tokugawa Yoshinobu kao.jpg | module = {{Infobox officeholder | embed = yes | office = ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' | termstart = 29 August 1866 | termend = 19 November 1867 | monarch = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|en|Emperor Kōmei|WD=Q299179|lt=Kōmei|1=Emperor Kōmei}} * {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}}} | predecessor = [[Tokugawa Iemochi]] | successor = ''{{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Position abolished|1=Bakumatsu}}''
[[Itō Hirobumi]] (as {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|WD=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister of Japan|1=Prime Minister of Japan}}) }} }} [[Kazoku|Prince]] {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Yoshinobu'''|德川 慶喜|4=also known as ''Keiki''; October 28, 1837 – November 22, 1913}} was the 15th and last ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. He was part of a movement which aimed to reform the aging shogunate, but was ultimately unsuccessful. He resigned his position as shogun in late 1867, while aiming at keeping some political influence. After these efforts failed following the defeat at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}} in early 1868, he went into retirement, and largely avoided the public eye for the rest of his life. ==Early life== Tokugawa Yoshinobu was born in {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}} as the seventh son of [[Tokugawa Nariaki]], ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of Mito. Mito was one of the ''{{ill|Gosanke|en|Gosanke|WD=Q1143543|lt=Gosanke|1=Gosanke}}'', the three branch families of the Tokugawa clan which were eligible to be chosen as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''. His birth name was Matsudaira Shichirōmaro ({{lang|ja|松平七郎麻呂}})Takano, ''Tokugawa Yoshinobu'', p. 26. Sons of the lord of Mito did not bear the name Tokugawa unless they themselves became the next lord. His mother, {{ill|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|en|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|WD=Q8944971|lt=Princess Arisugawa Yoshiko|1=Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)}}, was a member of the {{ill|Arisugawa-no-miya|en|Arisugawa-no-miya|WD=Q2861427|lt=Arisugawa-no-miya|1=Arisugawa-no-miya}}, a cadet branch of the imperial family; through her, he was a third cousin (once removed) of the then-{{ill|Emperor Ninkō|en|Emperor Ninkō|WD=Q312351|lt=Emperor Ninkō|1=Emperor Ninkō}}. Shichirōmaro was brought up under strict, spartan supervision and tutelage.Tokugawa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naishobanashi'', pp. 138–140. His father Nariaki followed the example of the second Mito daimyo, {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni|1=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} (1661-1690), who had sent all his sons after the firstborn to be raised in Mito. Shichirōmaro was seven months old when he arrived in Mito in 1838. He was taught in the literary and {{ill|Japanese martial arts|en|Japanese martial arts|WD=Q1280410|lt=martial arts|1=Japanese martial arts}}, as well as receiving a solid education in the principles of politics and government at {{ill|Kōdōkan (Mito)|en|Kōdōkan (Mito)|WD=Q3081773|lt=Kōdōkan|1=Kōdōkan (Mito)}}.Takano, p. 28. [[File:Tokugawa yoshinobu.jpg|thumb|250px|Yoshinobu in ceremonial dress]] At the instigation of his father, Shichirōmaro was adopted by the {{ill|Gosankyō|en|Gosankyō|WD=Q1143633|lt=Hitotsubashi-Tokugawa|1=Gosankyō}} family in order to have a better chance of succeeding to the shogunateTakano, p. 38. and changed his first name to [[:ja:昭致|Akimune]] (昭致). He became family head in 1847, coming of age that year, receiving court Rank and title, and taking the name Yoshinobu.Takano, p. 48. Upon the death of the 13th ''shōgun'', {{ill|Tokugawa Iesada|en|Tokugawa Iesada|WD=Q336383|lt=Iesada|1=Tokugawa Iesada}}, in 1858, Yoshinobu was nominated as a potential successor.Borton, ''Japan's Modern Century'', p. 40. His supporters touted his skill and efficiency in managing family affairs. However, the opposing faction, led by {{ill|Ii Naosuke|en|Ii Naosuke|WD=Q716940|lt=Ii Naosuke|1=Ii Naosuke}}, won out. Their candidate, the young [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshitomi|Tokugawa Yoshitomi]], was chosen, and became the 14th ''shōgun'' Iemochi.Borton, pp. 39–40. Soon after, during the {{ill|Ansei Purge|en|Ansei Purge|WD=Q569487|lt=Ansei Purge|1=Ansei Purge}}, Yoshinobu and others who supported him were placed under {{ill|House arrest|en|House arrest|WD=Q320994|lt=House arrest|1=House arrest}}.Takano, pp. 12–13. Yoshinobu himself was made to retire from Hitotsubashi headship. The period of Ii's domination of the Tokugawa government was marked by mismanagement and political infighting. Upon Ii's {{ill|Sakuradamon Incident (1860)|en|Sakuradamon Incident (1860)|WD=Q46603|lt=assassination|1=Sakuradamon Incident (1860)}} in 1860, Yoshinobu was reinstated as Hitotsubashi family head, and was nominated in 1862 to be the {{nihongo|''shōgun''{{'}}s guardian|将軍後見職|shōgun kōken-shoku}}, receiving the position soon afterwards.Murray, ''Japan'', p. 362; Kobiyama, ''Matsudaira Katamori no shōgai'', p. 75; Bolitho, ''Collapse of the Tokugawa Bakufu'', p. 9. At the same time, his two closest allies, {{ill|Matsudaira Yoshinaga|en|Matsudaira Yoshinaga|WD=Q910802|lt=Matsudaira Yoshinaga|1=Matsudaira Yoshinaga}} and {{ill|Matsudaira Katamori|en|Matsudaira Katamori|WD=Q569441|lt=Matsudaira Katamori|1=Matsudaira Katamori}}, were appointed to other high positions: Yoshinaga as {{nihongo|chief of political affairs|政治総裁職|seiji sōsai shoku}},Kobiyama, p. 75. Katamori as {{nihongo|Guardian of Kyoto|京都守護職|{{ill|Kyoto Shugoshoku|en|Kyoto Shugoshoku|WD=Q3130091|lt=Kyoto Shugoshoku|1=Kyoto Shugoshoku}}}}.Takano, pp. 132–133. The three men then took numerous steps to quell political unrest in the Kyoto area, and gathered allies to counter the activities of the rebellious {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}. They were instrumental figures in the ''{{ill|Kōbu gattai|en|Kōbu gattai|WD=Q1189374|lt=Kōbu gattai|1=Kōbu gattai}}'' political party, which sought a reconciliation between the shogunate and the imperial court.Kobiyama, pp. 84–87; Totman, p. 45; Takano, p. 20. In 1864, Yoshinobu, as commander of the imperial palace's defense, defeated the Chōshū forces in their attempt to capture the imperial palace's {{nihongo|Hamaguri Gate|蛤御門|Hamaguri-Gomon}} in what is called the [[:en:Kinmon Incident|Kinmon Incident]]. This was achieved by use of the forces of the {{ill|Aizu|en|Aizu|WD=Q1205071|lt=Aizu|1=Aizu}}–[[:en:Satsuma province|Satsuma]] coalition.See ''Japan 1853–1864, Or, Genji Yume Monogatari'', trans. by Ernest Mason Satow. (Tokyo: Naigai Shuppan Kyokai), for more. ==''Shōgun'' (1866–1867)== [[File:Members of French Military Mission to Japan in 1867.png|thumb|Members of the French military mission to Japan, invited by Tokugawa Yoshinobu for the modernization of his forces, in 1867]] After the death of [[Tokugawa Iemochi]] in 1866, Yoshinobu was chosen to succeed him, and became the 15th ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''.Borton, p. 63. He was the only Tokugawa ''shōgun'' to spend his entire tenure outside of Edo: he never set foot in {{ill|Edo Castle|en|Edo Castle|WD=Q865913|lt=Edo Castle|1=Edo Castle}} as ''shōgun''.Tokugawa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naishobanashi'', vol. 2, p. 162. Immediately upon Yoshinobu's ascension as ''shōgun'', major changes were initiated. A massive government overhaul was undertaken to initiate reforms that would strengthen the Tokugawa government. In particular, assistance from the {{ill|Second French Empire|en|Second French Empire|WD=Q71092|lt=Second French Empire|1=Second French Empire}} was organized, with the construction of the {{ill|Yokosuka|en|Yokosuka|WD=Q200578|lt=Yokosuka|1=Yokosuka}} arsenal under {{ill|Léonce Verny|en|Léonce Verny|WD=Q3091714|lt=Léonce Verny|1=Léonce Verny}}, and the dispatch of a {{ill|French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)|en|French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)|WD=Q3316839|lt=French military mission|1=French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)}} to modernize the armies of the ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''.Sims, ''French Policy Towards the Bakufu and Meiji Japan, 1854–95'', p. 236. The national army and navy, which had already been formed under Tokugawa command, were strengthened by the assistance of the Russians, and the {{ill|Tracey Mission|en|Tracey Mission|WD=Q7831253|lt=Tracey Mission|1=Tracey Mission}} provided by the British Royal Navy. Equipment was also purchased from the United States.Treat, ''Japan and the United States: 1853–1921'', p. 89 The outlook among many was that the Tokugawa Shogunate was gaining ground towards renewed strength and power; however, it fell in less than a year. ==Boshin War (1868–69)== {{Main|Boshin War}} Fearing the renewed strengthening of the Tokugawa shogunate under a strong and wise ruler, samurai from {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}}, {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū|1=Chōshū Domain}} and {{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|WD=Q1189704|lt=Tosa|1=Tosa Domain}} formed an alliance to counter it. Under the banner of ''[[sonnō jōi]]'' ("revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians!") coupled with a fear of the new ''shōgun'' as the "Rebirth of {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}" (家康の再来) who would continue to usurp the power of the Emperor, they worked to bring about an end to the shogunate, though they varied in their approaches. In particular, Tosa was more moderate; it proposed a compromise whereby Yoshinobu would resign as ''shōgun'', but preside over a new national governing council composed of various ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s''. To this end, Yamanouchi Toyonori, the lord of Tosa, together with his advisor, {{ill|Gotō Shōjirō|en|Gotō Shōjirō|WD=Q711721|lt=Gotō Shōjirō|1=Gotō Shōjirō}}, petitioned Yoshinobu to resign in order to make this possible.Beasley, ''The History of Modern Japan'', p. 96. On November 9, 1867, Yoshinobu tendered his resignation to the Emperor and formally stepped down ten days later, returning governing power to the Emperor.Takano, p. 256. He then withdrew from Kyoto to {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka}}. However, Satsuma and Chōshū, while supportive of a governing council of ''daimyōs'', were opposed to Yoshinobu's leading it. They secretly obtained an imperial edict calling for the use of force against Yoshinobu (later shown to be a {{ill|forgery|en|forgery|WD=Q1332286|lt=forgery|1=Forgery}})Yamakawa, ''Aizu Boshin Senshi'', pp. 7–9. and moved a massive number of Satsuma and Chōshū troops into Kyoto.Beasley, p. 97. There was a meeting called at the imperial court, where Yoshinobu was stripped of all titles and land,Beasley, p. 97; Yamakawa, ''Aizu Boshin Senshi'', p. 148–151. despite having taken no action that could be construed as aggressive or criminal. Any who would have opposed this were not included in the meeting. Yoshinobu opposed this action, and composed a message of protest, to be delivered to the imperial court;Totman, p. 416. For a copy of the original text of the message, see Yamakawa, pp. 89–90. at the urging of the leaders of Aizu, Kuwana, and other domains, and in light of the immense number of Satsuma and Chōshū troops in Kyoto, he dispatched a large body of troops to convey this message to the court.Totman, p. 417. When the Tokugawa forces arrived outside Kyoto, they were refused entry, and were attacked by Satsuma and Chōshū troops, starting the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, the first clash of the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}.Sasaki, pp. 23–24; Bolitho, pp. 420–422. Though the Tokugawa forces had a distinct advantage in numbers, Yoshinobu abandoned his army in the midst of the fight once he realized the Satsuma and Chōshū forces raised the Imperial banner, and escaped to {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}.Kobiyama, p. 124. He placed himself under voluntary confinement, and indicated his submission to the imperial court. However, a peace agreement was reached wherein [[:en:Tayasu Kamenosuke|Tayasu Kamenosuke]], the young head of a branch of the Tokugawa family, was adopted and made Tokugawa family head;Griffis, ''The Mikado: Institution and Person'', p. 141. On April 11, Edo Castle was handed over to the imperial army,Takano, p. 267.{{cite book|title=Tokyo, an administrative perspective|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBzAAAAIAAJ|access-date=9 April 2011|year=1958|publisher=Tokyo Metropolitan Government|page=21|archive-date=26 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140926054906/http://books.google.com/books?id=DoBzAAAAIAAJ|url-status=live}} and the city spared from all-out war. Together with Kamenosuke (who took the name {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|WD=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}), Yoshinobu moved to {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate, had also retired to Shizuoka, centuries earlier. Iesato was made the ''daimyō'' of the new [[:en:Shizuoka Domain|Shizuoka Domain]], but lost this title a few years later, when the domains were abolished. Even after losing his position as ruling shogun, Yoshinobu strove to promote his son Iesato's political career so that he could attain the highest level of influence in the Japanese Imperial court, and also serve as a bridge between old world Japan and modern emerging Japan both domestically and internationally. The close relationship between father and son is highlighted in the illustrated biography on Prince Tokugawa Iesato titled ''The Art of Peace''.{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2019|title=Introduction to The Art of Peace: the illustrated biography of Prince Iyesato Tokugawa|url=https://theemperorandthespy.com/2020/04/the-art-of-peace-the-illustrated-biography-on-prince-iyesato-tokugawa/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805132921/https://theemperorandthespy.com/2020/04/the-art-of-peace-the-illustrated-biography-on-prince-iyesato-tokugawa/|archive-date=2020-08-05|access-date=|website=TheEmperorAndTheSpy.com}} [[File:Yoshinobu Tokugawa 2.jpg|thumb|Tokugawa Yoshinobu in court uniform]] Many of the ''{{ill|Hatamoto|en|Hatamoto|WD=Q572662|lt=Hatamoto|1=Hatamoto}}'' also relocated to Shizuoka; a large proportion of them did not find adequate means to support themselves. As a result, many of them resented Yoshinobu, some of them to the point of wanting him dead.Tokugawa Munefusa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naisho banashi'', vol. 1, p. 131 Yoshinobu was aware of this, and was so afraid of assassination that he redesigned his sleeping arrangement to confuse any potential assassin.Tokugawa, pp. 131–133 ==Later life== [[File:Tokugawa Yoshinobu Kyudo with Yumi.jpg|thumb|Kyudo was one of his elaborate hobbies, and it is said that he continued to draw a bow every day until the spring of his 77th year.]] Living a life in quiet retirement, Yoshinobu indulged in many hobbies, including oil painting, [[:en:Kyudo|Kyudo]] (archery), hunting, photography, and cycling.Tokugawa, pp. 136–138. Some of Yoshinobu's photographs have been published in recent years by his great-grandson, {{ill|Yoshitomo Tokugawa|en|Yoshitomo Tokugawa|WD=Q7005100|lt=Yoshitomo|1=Yoshitomo Tokugawa}}.For an example of Yoshinobu's photography, see: Tokugawa Yoshitomo, ''Tokugawa Yoshinobu-ke e yōkoso'', p. 73. His other great-grandson, Yasuhisa Tokugawa of the Mito line, is the former Chief Priest at {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine|1=Yasukuni Shrine}} and current Kaicho of the [[:en:Kokusai Budoin|Kokusai Budoin]] (IMAF). In 1902, the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} allowed him to re-establish his own house as a Tokugawa branch (''bekke'') with the highest Rank in the peerage, that of prince (''kōshaku''), for his loyal service to Japan.Takano, p. 273. He took a seat in the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}, and resigned in 1910. Tokugawa Yoshinobu died on 21 November 1913 at 16:10 and is buried in {{ill|Yanaka Cemetery|en|Yanaka Cemetery|WD=Q864387|lt=Yanaka Cemetery|1=Yanaka Cemetery}}, Tokyo. On 9 January 1896, his ninth daughter Tsuneko Tokugawa (1882–1939) married {{ill|Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|en|Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|WD=Q285846|lt=Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|1=Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu}}, a second cousin to both {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Emperor Hirohito|1=Hirohito}} and {{ill|Empress Nagako|en|Empress Nagako|WD=Q230697|lt=Empress Nagako|1=Empress Nagako}} and nephew of {{ill|Prince Kan'in Kotohito|en|Prince Kan'in Kotohito|WD=Q701201|lt=Prince Kan'in Kotohito|1=Prince Kan'in Kotohito}}. On 26 December 1911, his granddaughter {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|WD=Q467655|lt=Kikuko Tokugawa|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} was born. She married [[:en:Prince Takamatsu|Prince Takamatsu]], the brother of Emperor Hirohito, to become Princess Takamatsu. 德川 慶喜 | image = 1867 Osaka Yoshinobu Tokugawa.jpg | caption = Tokugawa in 1867 | succession = Member of the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}} | reign-type = Tenure | reign = 1902–1910 | birth_date = {{birth date|1837|10|28}} | birth_place = {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}, Tokugawa Shogunate | death_date = {{death date and age|1913|11|22|1837|10|28}} | death_place = [[:en:Bunkyō, Tokyo|Bunkyō, Tokyo]], Empire Of Japan | burial_place = {{ill|Yanaka Cemetery|en|Yanaka Cemetery|WD=Q864387|lt=Yanaka Cemetery|1=Yanaka Cemetery}} | spouse = {{ill|Ichijo Mikako|jp|一条美賀子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichijo Mikako|qq=}} | house = [[Tokugawa clan]] | father = [[Tokugawa Nariaki]] | mother = {{ill|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|en|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|WD=Q8944971|lt=Arisugawa Yoshiko|1=Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)}} | signature = Tokugawa Yoshinobu kao.jpg | module = {{Infobox officeholder | embed = yes | office = ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' | termstart = 29 August 1866 | termend = 19 November 1867 | monarch = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|en|Emperor Kōmei|WD=Q299179|lt=Kōmei|1=Emperor Kōmei}} * {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}}} | predecessor = [[Tokugawa Iemochi]] | successor = ''{{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Position abolished|1=Bakumatsu}}''
[[Itō Hirobumi]] (as {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|WD=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister of Japan|1=Prime Minister of Japan}}) }} }} [[Kazoku|Prince]] {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Yoshinobu'''|德川 慶喜|4=also known as ''Keiki''; October 28, 1837 – November 22, 1913}} was the 15th and last ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. He was part of a movement which aimed to reform the aging shogunate, but was ultimately unsuccessful. He resigned his position as shogun in late 1867, while aiming at keeping some political influence. After these efforts failed following the defeat at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}} in early 1868, he went into retirement, and largely avoided the public eye for the rest of his life. ==Early life== Tokugawa Yoshinobu was born in {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}} as the seventh son of [[Tokugawa Nariaki]], ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of Mito. Mito was one of the ''{{ill|Gosanke|en|Gosanke|WD=Q1143543|lt=Gosanke|1=Gosanke}}'', the three branch families of the Tokugawa clan which were eligible to be chosen as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''. His birth name was Matsudaira Shichirōmaro ({{lang|ja|松平七郎麻呂}})Takano, ''Tokugawa Yoshinobu'', p. 26. Sons of the lord of Mito did not bear the name Tokugawa unless they themselves became the next lord. His mother, {{ill|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|en|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|WD=Q8944971|lt=Princess Arisugawa Yoshiko|1=Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)}}, was a member of the {{ill|Arisugawa-no-miya|en|Arisugawa-no-miya|WD=Q2861427|lt=Arisugawa-no-miya|1=Arisugawa-no-miya}}, a cadet branch of the imperial family; through her, he was a third cousin (once removed) of the then-{{ill|Emperor Ninkō|en|Emperor Ninkō|WD=Q312351|lt=Emperor Ninkō|1=Emperor Ninkō}}. Shichirōmaro was brought up under strict, spartan supervision and tutelage.Tokugawa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naishobanashi'', pp. 138–140. His father Nariaki followed the example of the second Mito daimyo, {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni|1=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} (1661-1690), who had sent all his sons after the firstborn to be raised in Mito. Shichirōmaro was seven months old when he arrived in Mito in 1838. He was taught in the literary and {{ill|Japanese martial arts|en|Japanese martial arts|WD=Q1280410|lt=martial arts|1=Japanese martial arts}}, as well as receiving a solid education in the principles of politics and government at {{ill|Kōdōkan (Mito)|en|Kōdōkan (Mito)|WD=Q3081773|lt=Kōdōkan|1=Kōdōkan (Mito)}}.Takano, p. 28. [[File:Tokugawa yoshinobu.jpg|thumb|250px|Yoshinobu in ceremonial dress]] At the instigation of his father, Shichirōmaro was adopted by the {{ill|Gosankyō|en|Gosankyō|WD=Q1143633|lt=Hitotsubashi-Tokugawa|1=Gosankyō}} family in order to have a better chance of succeeding to the shogunateTakano, p. 38. and changed his first name to [[:ja:昭致|Akimune]] (昭致). He became family head in 1847, coming of age that year, receiving court Rank and title, and taking the name Yoshinobu.Takano, p. 48. Upon the death of the 13th ''shōgun'', {{ill|Tokugawa Iesada|en|Tokugawa Iesada|WD=Q336383|lt=Iesada|1=Tokugawa Iesada}}, in 1858, Yoshinobu was nominated as a potential successor.Borton, ''Japan's Modern Century'', p. 40. His supporters touted his skill and efficiency in managing family affairs. However, the opposing faction, led by {{ill|Ii Naosuke|en|Ii Naosuke|WD=Q716940|lt=Ii Naosuke|1=Ii Naosuke}}, won out. Their candidate, the young [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshitomi|Tokugawa Yoshitomi]], was chosen, and became the 14th ''shōgun'' Iemochi.Borton, pp. 39–40. Soon after, during the {{ill|Ansei Purge|en|Ansei Purge|WD=Q569487|lt=Ansei Purge|1=Ansei Purge}}, Yoshinobu and others who supported him were placed under {{ill|House arrest|en|House arrest|WD=Q320994|lt=House arrest|1=House arrest}}.Takano, pp. 12–13. Yoshinobu himself was made to retire from Hitotsubashi headship. The period of Ii's domination of the Tokugawa government was marked by mismanagement and political infighting. Upon Ii's {{ill|Sakuradamon Incident (1860)|en|Sakuradamon Incident (1860)|WD=Q46603|lt=assassination|1=Sakuradamon Incident (1860)}} in 1860, Yoshinobu was reinstated as Hitotsubashi family head, and was nominated in 1862 to be the {{nihongo|''shōgun''{{'}}s guardian|将軍後見職|shōgun kōken-shoku}}, receiving the position soon afterwards.Murray, ''Japan'', p. 362; Kobiyama, ''Matsudaira Katamori no shōgai'', p. 75; Bolitho, ''Collapse of the Tokugawa Bakufu'', p. 9. At the same time, his two closest allies, {{ill|Matsudaira Yoshinaga|en|Matsudaira Yoshinaga|WD=Q910802|lt=Matsudaira Yoshinaga|1=Matsudaira Yoshinaga}} and {{ill|Matsudaira Katamori|en|Matsudaira Katamori|WD=Q569441|lt=Matsudaira Katamori|1=Matsudaira Katamori}}, were appointed to other high positions: Yoshinaga as {{nihongo|chief of political affairs|政治総裁職|seiji sōsai shoku}},Kobiyama, p. 75. Katamori as {{nihongo|Guardian of Kyoto|京都守護職|{{ill|Kyoto Shugoshoku|en|Kyoto Shugoshoku|WD=Q3130091|lt=Kyoto Shugoshoku|1=Kyoto Shugoshoku}}}}.Takano, pp. 132–133. The three men then took numerous steps to quell political unrest in the Kyoto area, and gathered allies to counter the activities of the rebellious {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}. They were instrumental figures in the ''{{ill|Kōbu gattai|en|Kōbu gattai|WD=Q1189374|lt=Kōbu gattai|1=Kōbu gattai}}'' political party, which sought a reconciliation between the shogunate and the imperial court.Kobiyama, pp. 84–87; Totman, p. 45; Takano, p. 20. In 1864, Yoshinobu, as commander of the imperial palace's defense, defeated the Chōshū forces in their attempt to capture the imperial palace's {{nihongo|Hamaguri Gate|蛤御門|Hamaguri-Gomon}} in what is called the [[:en:Kinmon Incident|Kinmon Incident]]. This was achieved by use of the forces of the {{ill|Aizu|en|Aizu|WD=Q1205071|lt=Aizu|1=Aizu}}–[[:en:Satsuma province|Satsuma]] coalition.See ''Japan 1853–1864, Or, Genji Yume Monogatari'', trans. by Ernest Mason Satow. (Tokyo: Naigai Shuppan Kyokai), for more. ==''Shōgun'' (1866–1867)== [[File:Members of French Military Mission to Japan in 1867.png|thumb|Members of the French military mission to Japan, invited by Tokugawa Yoshinobu for the modernization of his forces, in 1867]] After the death of [[Tokugawa Iemochi]] in 1866, Yoshinobu was chosen to succeed him, and became the 15th ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''.Borton, p. 63. He was the only Tokugawa ''shōgun'' to spend his entire tenure outside of Edo: he never set foot in {{ill|Edo Castle|en|Edo Castle|WD=Q865913|lt=Edo Castle|1=Edo Castle}} as ''shōgun''.Tokugawa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naishobanashi'', vol. 2, p. 162. Immediately upon Yoshinobu's ascension as ''shōgun'', major changes were initiated. A massive government overhaul was undertaken to initiate reforms that would strengthen the Tokugawa government. In particular, assistance from the {{ill|Second French Empire|en|Second French Empire|WD=Q71092|lt=Second French Empire|1=Second French Empire}} was organized, with the construction of the {{ill|Yokosuka|en|Yokosuka|WD=Q200578|lt=Yokosuka|1=Yokosuka}} arsenal under {{ill|Léonce Verny|en|Léonce Verny|WD=Q3091714|lt=Léonce Verny|1=Léonce Verny}}, and the dispatch of a {{ill|French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)|en|French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)|WD=Q3316839|lt=French military mission|1=French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)}} to modernize the armies of the ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''.Sims, ''French Policy Towards the Bakufu and Meiji Japan, 1854–95'', p. 236. The national army and navy, which had already been formed under Tokugawa command, were strengthened by the assistance of the Russians, and the {{ill|Tracey Mission|en|Tracey Mission|WD=Q7831253|lt=Tracey Mission|1=Tracey Mission}} provided by the British Royal Navy. Equipment was also purchased from the United States.Treat, ''Japan and the United States: 1853–1921'', p. 89 The outlook among many was that the Tokugawa Shogunate was gaining ground towards renewed strength and power; however, it fell in less than a year. ==Boshin War (1868–69)== {{Main|Boshin War}} Fearing the renewed strengthening of the Tokugawa shogunate under a strong and wise ruler, samurai from {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}}, {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū|1=Chōshū Domain}} and {{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|WD=Q1189704|lt=Tosa|1=Tosa Domain}} formed an alliance to counter it. Under the banner of ''[[sonnō jōi]]'' ("revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians!") coupled with a fear of the new ''shōgun'' as the "Rebirth of {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}" (家康の再来) who would continue to usurp the power of the Emperor, they worked to bring about an end to the shogunate, though they varied in their approaches. In particular, Tosa was more moderate; it proposed a compromise whereby Yoshinobu would resign as ''shōgun'', but preside over a new national governing council composed of various ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s''. To this end, Yamanouchi Toyonori, the lord of Tosa, together with his advisor, {{ill|Gotō Shōjirō|en|Gotō Shōjirō|WD=Q711721|lt=Gotō Shōjirō|1=Gotō Shōjirō}}, petitioned Yoshinobu to resign in order to make this possible.Beasley, ''The History of Modern Japan'', p. 96. On November 9, 1867, Yoshinobu tendered his resignation to the Emperor and formally stepped down ten days later, returning governing power to the Emperor.Takano, p. 256. He then withdrew from Kyoto to {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka}}. However, Satsuma and Chōshū, while supportive of a governing council of ''daimyōs'', were opposed to Yoshinobu's leading it. They secretly obtained an imperial edict calling for the use of force against Yoshinobu (later shown to be a {{ill|forgery|en|forgery|WD=Q1332286|lt=forgery|1=Forgery}})Yamakawa, ''Aizu Boshin Senshi'', pp. 7–9. and moved a massive number of Satsuma and Chōshū troops into Kyoto.Beasley, p. 97. There was a meeting called at the imperial court, where Yoshinobu was stripped of all titles and land,Beasley, p. 97; Yamakawa, ''Aizu Boshin Senshi'', p. 148–151. despite having taken no action that could be construed as aggressive or criminal. Any who would have opposed this were not included in the meeting. Yoshinobu opposed this action, and composed a message of protest, to be delivered to the imperial court;Totman, p. 416. For a copy of the original text of the message, see Yamakawa, pp. 89–90. at the urging of the leaders of Aizu, Kuwana, and other domains, and in light of the immense number of Satsuma and Chōshū troops in Kyoto, he dispatched a large body of troops to convey this message to the court.Totman, p. 417. When the Tokugawa forces arrived outside Kyoto, they were refused entry, and were attacked by Satsuma and Chōshū troops, starting the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, the first clash of the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}.Sasaki, pp. 23–24; Bolitho, pp. 420–422. Though the Tokugawa forces had a distinct advantage in numbers, Yoshinobu abandoned his army in the midst of the fight once he realized the Satsuma and Chōshū forces raised the Imperial banner, and escaped to {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}.Kobiyama, p. 124. He placed himself under voluntary confinement, and indicated his submission to the imperial court. However, a peace agreement was reached wherein [[:en:Tayasu Kamenosuke|Tayasu Kamenosuke]], the young head of a branch of the Tokugawa family, was adopted and made Tokugawa family head;Griffis, ''The Mikado: Institution and Person'', p. 141. On April 11, Edo Castle was handed over to the imperial army,Takano, p. 267.{{cite book|title=Tokyo, an administrative perspective|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBzAAAAIAAJ|access-date=9 April 2011|year=1958|publisher=Tokyo Metropolitan Government|page=21|archive-date=26 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140926054906/http://books.google.com/books?id=DoBzAAAAIAAJ|url-status=live}} and the city spared from all-out war. Together with Kamenosuke (who took the name {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|WD=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}), Yoshinobu moved to {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate, had also retired to Shizuoka, centuries earlier. Iesato was made the ''daimyō'' of the new [[:en:Shizuoka Domain|Shizuoka Domain]], but lost this title a few years later, when the domains were abolished. Even after losing his position as ruling shogun, Yoshinobu strove to promote his son Iesato's political career so that he could attain the highest level of influence in the Japanese Imperial court, and also serve as a bridge between old world Japan and modern emerging Japan both domestically and internationally. The close relationship between father and son is highlighted in the illustrated biography on Prince Tokugawa Iesato titled ''The Art of Peace''.{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2019|title=Introduction to The Art of Peace: the illustrated biography of Prince Iyesato Tokugawa|url=https://theemperorandthespy.com/2020/04/the-art-of-peace-the-illustrated-biography-on-prince-iyesato-tokugawa/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805132921/https://theemperorandthespy.com/2020/04/the-art-of-peace-the-illustrated-biography-on-prince-iyesato-tokugawa/|archive-date=2020-08-05|access-date=|website=TheEmperorAndTheSpy.com}} [[File:Yoshinobu Tokugawa 2.jpg|thumb|Tokugawa Yoshinobu in court uniform]] Many of the ''{{ill|Hatamoto|en|Hatamoto|WD=Q572662|lt=Hatamoto|1=Hatamoto}}'' also relocated to Shizuoka; a large proportion of them did not find adequate means to support themselves. As a result, many of them resented Yoshinobu, some of them to the point of wanting him dead.Tokugawa Munefusa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naisho banashi'', vol. 1, p. 131 Yoshinobu was aware of this, and was so afraid of assassination that he redesigned his sleeping arrangement to confuse any potential assassin.Tokugawa, pp. 131–133 ==Later life== [[File:Tokugawa Yoshinobu Kyudo with Yumi.jpg|thumb|Kyudo was one of his elaborate hobbies, and it is said that he continued to draw a bow every day until the spring of his 77th year.]] Living a life in quiet retirement, Yoshinobu indulged in many hobbies, including oil painting, [[:en:Kyudo|Kyudo]] (archery), hunting, photography, and cycling.Tokugawa, pp. 136–138. Some of Yoshinobu's photographs have been published in recent years by his great-grandson, {{ill|Yoshitomo Tokugawa|en|Yoshitomo Tokugawa|WD=Q7005100|lt=Yoshitomo|1=Yoshitomo Tokugawa}}.For an example of Yoshinobu's photography, see: Tokugawa Yoshitomo, ''Tokugawa Yoshinobu-ke e yōkoso'', p. 73. His other great-grandson, Yasuhisa Tokugawa of the Mito line, is the former Chief Priest at {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine|1=Yasukuni Shrine}} and current Kaicho of the [[:en:Kokusai Budoin|Kokusai Budoin]] (IMAF). In 1902, the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} allowed him to re-establish his own house as a Tokugawa branch (''bekke'') with the highest Rank in the peerage, that of prince (''kōshaku''), for his loyal service to Japan.Takano, p. 273. He took a seat in the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}, and resigned in 1910. Tokugawa Yoshinobu died on 21 November 1913 at 16:10 and is buried in {{ill|Yanaka Cemetery|en|Yanaka Cemetery|WD=Q864387|lt=Yanaka Cemetery|1=Yanaka Cemetery}}, Tokyo. On 9 January 1896, his ninth daughter Tsuneko Tokugawa (1882–1939) married {{ill|Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|en|Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|WD=Q285846|lt=Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|1=Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu}}, a second cousin to both {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Emperor Hirohito|1=Hirohito}} and {{ill|Empress Nagako|en|Empress Nagako|WD=Q230697|lt=Empress Nagako|1=Empress Nagako}} and nephew of {{ill|Prince Kan'in Kotohito|en|Prince Kan'in Kotohito|WD=Q701201|lt=Prince Kan'in Kotohito|1=Prince Kan'in Kotohito}}. On 26 December 1911, his granddaughter {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|WD=Q467655|lt=Kikuko Tokugawa|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} was born. She married [[:en:Prince Takamatsu|Prince Takamatsu]], the brother of Emperor Hirohito, to become Princess Takamatsu. Shrapnel cut down Tokugawa and two enlisted lookouts, but the submarine was able to dive and escape. 德川 慶喜 | image = 1867 Osaka Yoshinobu Tokugawa.jpg | caption = Tokugawa in 1867 | succession = Member of the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}} | reign-type = Tenure | reign = 1902–1910 | birth_date = {{birth date|1837|10|28}} | birth_place = {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}, Tokugawa Shogunate | death_date = {{death date and age|1913|11|22|1837|10|28}} | death_place = [[:en:Bunkyō, Tokyo|Bunkyō, Tokyo]], Empire Of Japan | burial_place = {{ill|Yanaka Cemetery|en|Yanaka Cemetery|WD=Q864387|lt=Yanaka Cemetery|1=Yanaka Cemetery}} | spouse = {{ill|Ichijo Mikako|jp|一条美賀子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichijo Mikako|qq=}} | house = [[Tokugawa clan]] | father = [[Tokugawa Nariaki]] | mother = {{ill|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|en|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|WD=Q8944971|lt=Arisugawa Yoshiko|1=Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)}} | signature = Tokugawa Yoshinobu kao.jpg | module = {{Infobox officeholder | embed = yes | office = ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' | termstart = 29 August 1866 | termend = 19 November 1867 | monarch = {{Plainlist| * {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|en|Emperor Kōmei|WD=Q299179|lt=Kōmei|1=Emperor Kōmei}} * {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}}} | predecessor = [[Tokugawa Iemochi]] | successor = ''{{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Position abolished|1=Bakumatsu}}''
[[Itō Hirobumi]] (as {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|WD=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister of Japan|1=Prime Minister of Japan}}) }} }} [[Kazoku|Prince]] {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Yoshinobu'''|德川 慶喜|4=also known as ''Keiki''; October 28, 1837 – November 22, 1913}} was the 15th and last ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. He was part of a movement which aimed to reform the aging shogunate, but was ultimately unsuccessful. He resigned his position as shogun in late 1867, while aiming at keeping some political influence. After these efforts failed following the defeat at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}} in early 1868, he went into retirement, and largely avoided the public eye for the rest of his life. ==Early life== Tokugawa Yoshinobu was born in {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}} as the seventh son of [[Tokugawa Nariaki]], ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of Mito. Mito was one of the ''{{ill|Gosanke|en|Gosanke|WD=Q1143543|lt=Gosanke|1=Gosanke}}'', the three branch families of the Tokugawa clan which were eligible to be chosen as ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''. His birth name was Matsudaira Shichirōmaro ({{lang|ja|松平七郎麻呂}})Takano, ''Tokugawa Yoshinobu'', p. 26. Sons of the lord of Mito did not bear the name Tokugawa unless they themselves became the next lord. His mother, {{ill|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|en|Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)|WD=Q8944971|lt=Princess Arisugawa Yoshiko|1=Princess Yoshiko (Arisugawa-no-miya)}}, was a member of the {{ill|Arisugawa-no-miya|en|Arisugawa-no-miya|WD=Q2861427|lt=Arisugawa-no-miya|1=Arisugawa-no-miya}}, a cadet branch of the imperial family; through her, he was a third cousin (once removed) of the then-{{ill|Emperor Ninkō|en|Emperor Ninkō|WD=Q312351|lt=Emperor Ninkō|1=Emperor Ninkō}}. Shichirōmaro was brought up under strict, spartan supervision and tutelage.Tokugawa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naishobanashi'', pp. 138–140. His father Nariaki followed the example of the second Mito daimyo, {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni|1=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}} (1661-1690), who had sent all his sons after the firstborn to be raised in Mito. Shichirōmaro was seven months old when he arrived in Mito in 1838. He was taught in the literary and {{ill|Japanese martial arts|en|Japanese martial arts|WD=Q1280410|lt=martial arts|1=Japanese martial arts}}, as well as receiving a solid education in the principles of politics and government at {{ill|Kōdōkan (Mito)|en|Kōdōkan (Mito)|WD=Q3081773|lt=Kōdōkan|1=Kōdōkan (Mito)}}.Takano, p. 28. [[File:Tokugawa yoshinobu.jpg|thumb|250px|Yoshinobu in ceremonial dress]] At the instigation of his father, Shichirōmaro was adopted by the {{ill|Gosankyō|en|Gosankyō|WD=Q1143633|lt=Hitotsubashi-Tokugawa|1=Gosankyō}} family in order to have a better chance of succeeding to the shogunateTakano, p. 38. and changed his first name to [[:ja:昭致|Akimune]] (昭致). He became family head in 1847, coming of age that year, receiving court Rank and title, and taking the name Yoshinobu.Takano, p. 48. Upon the death of the 13th ''shōgun'', {{ill|Tokugawa Iesada|en|Tokugawa Iesada|WD=Q336383|lt=Iesada|1=Tokugawa Iesada}}, in 1858, Yoshinobu was nominated as a potential successor.Borton, ''Japan's Modern Century'', p. 40. His supporters touted his skill and efficiency in managing family affairs. However, the opposing faction, led by {{ill|Ii Naosuke|en|Ii Naosuke|WD=Q716940|lt=Ii Naosuke|1=Ii Naosuke}}, won out. Their candidate, the young [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshitomi|Tokugawa Yoshitomi]], was chosen, and became the 14th ''shōgun'' Iemochi.Borton, pp. 39–40. Soon after, during the {{ill|Ansei Purge|en|Ansei Purge|WD=Q569487|lt=Ansei Purge|1=Ansei Purge}}, Yoshinobu and others who supported him were placed under {{ill|House arrest|en|House arrest|WD=Q320994|lt=House arrest|1=House arrest}}.Takano, pp. 12–13. Yoshinobu himself was made to retire from Hitotsubashi headship. The period of Ii's domination of the Tokugawa government was marked by mismanagement and political infighting. Upon Ii's {{ill|Sakuradamon Incident (1860)|en|Sakuradamon Incident (1860)|WD=Q46603|lt=assassination|1=Sakuradamon Incident (1860)}} in 1860, Yoshinobu was reinstated as Hitotsubashi family head, and was nominated in 1862 to be the {{nihongo|''shōgun''{{'}}s guardian|将軍後見職|shōgun kōken-shoku}}, receiving the position soon afterwards.Murray, ''Japan'', p. 362; Kobiyama, ''Matsudaira Katamori no shōgai'', p. 75; Bolitho, ''Collapse of the Tokugawa Bakufu'', p. 9. At the same time, his two closest allies, {{ill|Matsudaira Yoshinaga|en|Matsudaira Yoshinaga|WD=Q910802|lt=Matsudaira Yoshinaga|1=Matsudaira Yoshinaga}} and {{ill|Matsudaira Katamori|en|Matsudaira Katamori|WD=Q569441|lt=Matsudaira Katamori|1=Matsudaira Katamori}}, were appointed to other high positions: Yoshinaga as {{nihongo|chief of political affairs|政治総裁職|seiji sōsai shoku}},Kobiyama, p. 75. Katamori as {{nihongo|Guardian of Kyoto|京都守護職|{{ill|Kyoto Shugoshoku|en|Kyoto Shugoshoku|WD=Q3130091|lt=Kyoto Shugoshoku|1=Kyoto Shugoshoku}}}}.Takano, pp. 132–133. The three men then took numerous steps to quell political unrest in the Kyoto area, and gathered allies to counter the activities of the rebellious {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}. They were instrumental figures in the ''{{ill|Kōbu gattai|en|Kōbu gattai|WD=Q1189374|lt=Kōbu gattai|1=Kōbu gattai}}'' political party, which sought a reconciliation between the shogunate and the imperial court.Kobiyama, pp. 84–87; Totman, p. 45; Takano, p. 20. In 1864, Yoshinobu, as commander of the imperial palace's defense, defeated the Chōshū forces in their attempt to capture the imperial palace's {{nihongo|Hamaguri Gate|蛤御門|Hamaguri-Gomon}} in what is called the [[:en:Kinmon Incident|Kinmon Incident]]. This was achieved by use of the forces of the {{ill|Aizu|en|Aizu|WD=Q1205071|lt=Aizu|1=Aizu}}–[[:en:Satsuma province|Satsuma]] coalition.See ''Japan 1853–1864, Or, Genji Yume Monogatari'', trans. by Ernest Mason Satow. (Tokyo: Naigai Shuppan Kyokai), for more. ==''Shōgun'' (1866–1867)== [[File:Members of French Military Mission to Japan in 1867.png|thumb|Members of the French military mission to Japan, invited by Tokugawa Yoshinobu for the modernization of his forces, in 1867]] After the death of [[Tokugawa Iemochi]] in 1866, Yoshinobu was chosen to succeed him, and became the 15th ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''.Borton, p. 63. He was the only Tokugawa ''shōgun'' to spend his entire tenure outside of Edo: he never set foot in {{ill|Edo Castle|en|Edo Castle|WD=Q865913|lt=Edo Castle|1=Edo Castle}} as ''shōgun''.Tokugawa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naishobanashi'', vol. 2, p. 162. Immediately upon Yoshinobu's ascension as ''shōgun'', major changes were initiated. A massive government overhaul was undertaken to initiate reforms that would strengthen the Tokugawa government. In particular, assistance from the {{ill|Second French Empire|en|Second French Empire|WD=Q71092|lt=Second French Empire|1=Second French Empire}} was organized, with the construction of the {{ill|Yokosuka|en|Yokosuka|WD=Q200578|lt=Yokosuka|1=Yokosuka}} arsenal under {{ill|Léonce Verny|en|Léonce Verny|WD=Q3091714|lt=Léonce Verny|1=Léonce Verny}}, and the dispatch of a {{ill|French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)|en|French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)|WD=Q3316839|lt=French military mission|1=French military mission to Japan (1867–1868)}} to modernize the armies of the ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}''.Sims, ''French Policy Towards the Bakufu and Meiji Japan, 1854–95'', p. 236. The national army and navy, which had already been formed under Tokugawa command, were strengthened by the assistance of the Russians, and the {{ill|Tracey Mission|en|Tracey Mission|WD=Q7831253|lt=Tracey Mission|1=Tracey Mission}} provided by the British Royal Navy. Equipment was also purchased from the United States.Treat, ''Japan and the United States: 1853–1921'', p. 89 The outlook among many was that the Tokugawa Shogunate was gaining ground towards renewed strength and power; however, it fell in less than a year. ==Boshin War (1868–69)== {{Main|Boshin War}} Fearing the renewed strengthening of the Tokugawa shogunate under a strong and wise ruler, samurai from {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}}, {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū|1=Chōshū Domain}} and {{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|WD=Q1189704|lt=Tosa|1=Tosa Domain}} formed an alliance to counter it. Under the banner of ''[[sonnō jōi]]'' ("revere the Emperor, expel the barbarians!") coupled with a fear of the new ''shōgun'' as the "Rebirth of {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}" (家康の再来) who would continue to usurp the power of the Emperor, they worked to bring about an end to the shogunate, though they varied in their approaches. In particular, Tosa was more moderate; it proposed a compromise whereby Yoshinobu would resign as ''shōgun'', but preside over a new national governing council composed of various ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s''. To this end, Yamanouchi Toyonori, the lord of Tosa, together with his advisor, {{ill|Gotō Shōjirō|en|Gotō Shōjirō|WD=Q711721|lt=Gotō Shōjirō|1=Gotō Shōjirō}}, petitioned Yoshinobu to resign in order to make this possible.Beasley, ''The History of Modern Japan'', p. 96. On November 9, 1867, Yoshinobu tendered his resignation to the Emperor and formally stepped down ten days later, returning governing power to the Emperor.Takano, p. 256. He then withdrew from Kyoto to {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka}}. However, Satsuma and Chōshū, while supportive of a governing council of ''daimyōs'', were opposed to Yoshinobu's leading it. They secretly obtained an imperial edict calling for the use of force against Yoshinobu (later shown to be a {{ill|forgery|en|forgery|WD=Q1332286|lt=forgery|1=Forgery}})Yamakawa, ''Aizu Boshin Senshi'', pp. 7–9. and moved a massive number of Satsuma and Chōshū troops into Kyoto.Beasley, p. 97. There was a meeting called at the imperial court, where Yoshinobu was stripped of all titles and land,Beasley, p. 97; Yamakawa, ''Aizu Boshin Senshi'', p. 148–151. despite having taken no action that could be construed as aggressive or criminal. Any who would have opposed this were not included in the meeting. Yoshinobu opposed this action, and composed a message of protest, to be delivered to the imperial court;Totman, p. 416. For a copy of the original text of the message, see Yamakawa, pp. 89–90. at the urging of the leaders of Aizu, Kuwana, and other domains, and in light of the immense number of Satsuma and Chōshū troops in Kyoto, he dispatched a large body of troops to convey this message to the court.Totman, p. 417. When the Tokugawa forces arrived outside Kyoto, they were refused entry, and were attacked by Satsuma and Chōshū troops, starting the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, the first clash of the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}.Sasaki, pp. 23–24; Bolitho, pp. 420–422. Though the Tokugawa forces had a distinct advantage in numbers, Yoshinobu abandoned his army in the midst of the fight once he realized the Satsuma and Chōshū forces raised the Imperial banner, and escaped to {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}.Kobiyama, p. 124. He placed himself under voluntary confinement, and indicated his submission to the imperial court. However, a peace agreement was reached wherein [[:en:Tayasu Kamenosuke|Tayasu Kamenosuke]], the young head of a branch of the Tokugawa family, was adopted and made Tokugawa family head;Griffis, ''The Mikado: Institution and Person'', p. 141. On April 11, Edo Castle was handed over to the imperial army,Takano, p. 267.{{cite book|title=Tokyo, an administrative perspective|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBzAAAAIAAJ|access-date=9 April 2011|year=1958|publisher=Tokyo Metropolitan Government|page=21|archive-date=26 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140926054906/http://books.google.com/books?id=DoBzAAAAIAAJ|url-status=live}} and the city spared from all-out war. Together with Kamenosuke (who took the name {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|WD=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}), Yoshinobu moved to {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka|1=Shizuoka Prefecture}}. {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate, had also retired to Shizuoka, centuries earlier. Iesato was made the ''daimyō'' of the new [[:en:Shizuoka Domain|Shizuoka Domain]], but lost this title a few years later, when the domains were abolished. Even after losing his position as ruling shogun, Yoshinobu strove to promote his son Iesato's political career so that he could attain the highest level of influence in the Japanese Imperial court, and also serve as a bridge between old world Japan and modern emerging Japan both domestically and internationally. The close relationship between father and son is highlighted in the illustrated biography on Prince Tokugawa Iesato titled ''The Art of Peace''.{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2019|title=Introduction to The Art of Peace: the illustrated biography of Prince Iyesato Tokugawa|url=https://theemperorandthespy.com/2020/04/the-art-of-peace-the-illustrated-biography-on-prince-iyesato-tokugawa/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805132921/https://theemperorandthespy.com/2020/04/the-art-of-peace-the-illustrated-biography-on-prince-iyesato-tokugawa/|archive-date=2020-08-05|access-date=|website=TheEmperorAndTheSpy.com}} [[File:Yoshinobu Tokugawa 2.jpg|thumb|Tokugawa Yoshinobu in court uniform]] Many of the ''{{ill|Hatamoto|en|Hatamoto|WD=Q572662|lt=Hatamoto|1=Hatamoto}}'' also relocated to Shizuoka; a large proportion of them did not find adequate means to support themselves. As a result, many of them resented Yoshinobu, some of them to the point of wanting him dead.Tokugawa Munefusa, ''Tokugawa yonbyakunen no naisho banashi'', vol. 1, p. 131 Yoshinobu was aware of this, and was so afraid of assassination that he redesigned his sleeping arrangement to confuse any potential assassin.Tokugawa, pp. 131–133 ==Later life== [[File:Tokugawa Yoshinobu Kyudo with Yumi.jpg|thumb|Kyudo was one of his elaborate hobbies, and it is said that he continued to draw a bow every day until the spring of his 77th year.]] Living a life in quiet retirement, Yoshinobu indulged in many hobbies, including oil painting, [[:en:Kyudo|Kyudo]] (archery), hunting, photography, and cycling.Tokugawa, pp. 136–138. Some of Yoshinobu's photographs have been published in recent years by his great-grandson, {{ill|Yoshitomo Tokugawa|en|Yoshitomo Tokugawa|WD=Q7005100|lt=Yoshitomo|1=Yoshitomo Tokugawa}}.For an example of Yoshinobu's photography, see: Tokugawa Yoshitomo, ''Tokugawa Yoshinobu-ke e yōkoso'', p. 73. His other great-grandson, Yasuhisa Tokugawa of the Mito line, is the former Chief Priest at {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine|1=Yasukuni Shrine}} and current Kaicho of the [[:en:Kokusai Budoin|Kokusai Budoin]] (IMAF). In 1902, the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} allowed him to re-establish his own house as a Tokugawa branch (''bekke'') with the highest Rank in the peerage, that of prince (''kōshaku''), for his loyal service to Japan.Takano, p. 273. He took a seat in the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|WD=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}, and resigned in 1910. Tokugawa Yoshinobu died on 21 November 1913 at 16:10 and is buried in {{ill|Yanaka Cemetery|en|Yanaka Cemetery|WD=Q864387|lt=Yanaka Cemetery|1=Yanaka Cemetery}}, Tokyo. On 9 January 1896, his ninth daughter Tsuneko Tokugawa (1882–1939) married {{ill|Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|en|Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|WD=Q285846|lt=Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu|1=Prince Fushimi Hiroyasu}}, a second cousin to both {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Emperor Hirohito|1=Hirohito}} and {{ill|Empress Nagako|en|Empress Nagako|WD=Q230697|lt=Empress Nagako|1=Empress Nagako}} and nephew of {{ill|Prince Kan'in Kotohito|en|Prince Kan'in Kotohito|WD=Q701201|lt=Prince Kan'in Kotohito|1=Prince Kan'in Kotohito}}. On 26 December 1911, his granddaughter {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|WD=Q467655|lt=Kikuko Tokugawa|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} was born. She married [[:en:Prince Takamatsu|Prince Takamatsu]], the brother of Emperor Hirohito, to become Princess Takamatsu.
